Dans le voisinage de Milton Parc, des pe: In the Milton Parc neighbourhood, people who have experienced homelessness are working together to help the community living on the street. In the 2010s, Chris Brown panhandled near the Provigo at the corner of Milton and Parc. Now, this Cree man from Saskatchewan is a street outreach worker in the neighbourhood.
D’après son expérience, les personnes qu: From his experience, people living on the street in Montréal have built a tight-knit community. “Everybody knows everybody. When you use the organizations around downtown, like Projets Autochtones du Québec or the Native Friendship Centre, you walk into those spaces, and we all know each other by our first names. When someone in the community dies, we recognize the person right away. It hits us hard because of the difficult experiences we've all been through,” Chris explains in English.
« Pour ce qui est de la population autoc: “When it comes to the Indigenous population, the Inuit, there's a tendency among people from the North who get off the plane, and they know Montréal through messages and contacts, family and friends, who tell them: ‘Meet me at Parc Avenue, you'll see me, ask around and you'll find me,’” says Chris Brown.
Depuis quelques mois, Chris travaille po: For the past few months, Chris has been working for <l1>Comm-Un</l1>, a community organization that works with people living on the street in Milton Parc. At 3516 Parc Avenue, two green doors lead to an “office” on the left, where volunteers, street workers and people experiencing homelessness can chat, use a computer, trade jokes or get a cigarette. The centre also has a small kitchen and a bathroom. At the back, there's also a library with a large table where people sit down to work, sculpt or draw. Out the back door, there's a picnic table and, often, a group smoking cigarettes and chatting.
Comm-Un est le lieu de rencontre d’une é: Comm-Un is the meeting place for a street outreach team set up this year thanks to new funding. The team is made up mostly of people who were previously homeless in Milton Parc. It patrols Monday to Friday from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m.
« Nous sommes tous connus de la communau: “We're all known in the community, people trust us. Instead of someone from another organization who doesn't really know street life, they'll open up more to us,” says Chris.
‍<strong>Enlever le <em>feeling</em> de: ‍Getting rid of the feeling of being a stranger
Jonathan Lebire et Chris Brown travaille: Jonathan Lebire and Chris Brown work at Comm-Un. Photo: Emelia Fournier
Jonathan Lebire, le fondateur et directe: Jonathan Lebire, the founder and director of Comm-Un, has also been homeless. He was homeless as a teenager, and has since gained more than 20 years of experience as a street worker. Recognized by everyone who walks through Comm-Un's door, with his long grey hair tied in a ponytail and a smile on his face, Jonathan is ready to help.
« Quand on dit à quelqu’un : “Arrête de: “When you tell someone, ‘Stop drinking, get off the street,’ that's what most people think the equation should be. But that means you don't understand that this person has already tried many times, that it doesn't work, that there are other reasons they're there. These are human beings with a story that goes beyond substance use, beyond the crisis,” Jonathan tells us in an empty room at Comm-Un, to avoid being interrupted by the day-to-day requests.
Il aimerait que la communauté itinérante: He would like the homeless community of Milton Parc to be able to live in harmony with the broader community in the neighbourhood. “I know the people on the street in Milton Parc want to take part, they just don't know how. I think it's easier to start here, with our organization,” he says.
Il estime que la relation est maintenant: He believes that relations between housed and unhoused neighbours have become friendlier over the past two years. “I think we've worked a lot with everyone – Open Door, the other organizations – precisely to meet each other and get to know each other, and to get rid of the feeling of being a stranger, and of polarization,” explains Jonathan, energized by this change. “People know each other by name now. That makes a big difference,” he adds.
Un jeudi soir de janvier, Comm-Un anime: On a Thursday evening in January, Comm-Un hosts an activity in collaboration with Santropol Roulant, a community food centre that seeks to build connections between neighbours. Outside, across from Santropol Roulant, passersby from Roy Street join unhoused people from Milton Parc to listen to their stories and warm up by the fire. Inside, soup and hot drinks are offered to everyone.
Autour du feu, Junior, un homme de Kuujj: Around the fire, Junior, a man from Kuujjuaq, shares the joys of hunting and fishing in the North. Then Sam, an Inuk man, talks about his healing journey. He is getting ready to go to Waseskun, an Indigenous treatment centre, for a few months. Neighbourhood children slide down a snow mound next to him, while their parents watch Sim, an Inuk artist, make an ice sculpture.
« L’intention, c’est d’apporter des ress: “The intention is to bring resources, to get everyone on the same vibe, but really for the people who need it most,” sums up Jonathan.
<strong>Trouver un appartement sans perd: Finding an apartment without losing your community
De retour sur l’avenue du Parc, Chris no: Back on Parc Avenue, Chris tells us about the difficulties he faces as he moves out of homelessness.
Il a un domicile, mais avec les loyers e: He has a home, but with rents constantly going up, he can't afford an apartment closer to his community. “I have an apartment in Lachine, it's social housing, and I barely make ends meet, even with my two jobs. I work at a café too. I travel a lot, Lachine is pretty far, groceries are expensive. But I know a lot of organizations where I can find cheaper food, community fridges. You have to use the help that's available.”
Même avec ses difficultés financières, C: Even with his financial difficulties, Chris thinks other people can get off the street. In his view, homelessness “is an issue we all need to keep in mind.” “By helping each other, we can overcome these challenges. Homelessness isn't a dead end for everyone here. It's just a bump in the road. I got through it, even if the road is still a little bumpy. But at least everything gets better when you mind your own business and you have organizations to help you.”
Chato René Rivas Melara, un artiste maya: Chato René Rivas Melara, a Mayan artist, has a tenant experience similar to Chris's. Chato is from El Salvador. He ended up on the street in the Milton Parc neighbourhood a few years ago. Although he now has an apartment, he spends most of his time on the Plateau, with his chosen family.
« Maintenant, j’ai mon propre appartemen: “Now I have my own apartment with my dog, it's a very safe place to live, but I'm still on the street. I mean, I have my apartment, but my life is being on the street and helping these people.”
Chato a déménagé trois fois au cours des: Chato has moved three times in recent years because of rising rents. “I live far away, I live in Laval. So it's like they displace people from their homes, we are displaced people. That's why folks in Milton Parc, on the Plateau-Mont-Royal, or downtown are on the street – it's because we have no other option,” says Chato, disappointed.
Le lendemain, au coin de Rachel et de Pa: The next day, at the corner of Rachel and Papineau, we meet Chato at the Tlachiuak art workshop. He coordinates the space to offer refuge and healing to the homeless community. With the help of Comm-Un, the art workshop opened in mid-January in a basement room of the Immaculée-Conception parish church. “‘Tlachiuak’ means solidarity in the Nahuat language. We are like in union, the oscillation of people and of the circle of life,” Chato explains in English.
En nous guidant à travers l’espace, il n: Guiding us through the space, he shows us a table full of handmade Mayan jewellery, a sculpting station with low tables and tools, percussion instruments, a sewing machine, paintbrushes, paint and other art supplies. “Creating is part of being human. [It lets you] focus, forget things, bad things and traumatic things, you know, alcohol, or even work. If you work too much at the office, you can make art and you can express yourself,” Chato tells us in a soft but passionate voice.
Deux artistes inuit de Milton Parc, Sim: Two Inuit artists from Milton Parc, Sim and Nathan, carve soapstone with Andres Hasbun, Chato's friend and co-organizer of the workshop.
Andres a commencé à travailler avec Comm: Andres only recently started working with Comm-Un. He moved to Montréal in the 2010s and now has a family and a home in Ahuntsic. Before that, in El Salvador, Andres was homeless. “I'm also grateful for my difficult past, for what I've lived through. I was on the street too. I've been doing well for 10 years now, so I want to help others,” he says.
Les efforts de Chato et d’Andres sont ap: Chato and Andres's efforts are appreciated by people in Milton Parc's homeless community. “People tell me they feel better and they're happy in the space. [...] They say it feels good, that it's a caring space,” says Chato with a smile.
Nathan, un des sculpteurs inuit, polit u: Nathan, one of the Inuit sculptors, is polishing a small soapstone inukshuk. It's his first visit to the workshop. Without interrupting his work, he tells me the workshop is “very beautiful.” “I can carve inside, because it's cold outside. I like the space, because I can work,” he adds.
En occupant une salle dans une église, C: By occupying a room in a church, Chato believes the Indigenous community is reclaiming its place. “That's why I'm trying to create this space. It's to return to the culture, because we never disappeared. We're still here, we make things, in the church, these are beautiful things to do,” he confides. For him, occupying a room in a church is a way for Indigenous communities to take back space in the institution that dispossessed them. “We never forget it, we never disappeared.”
Par le biais du travail de rue, des évén: Through street outreach, community events and art, Chris Brown, Jonathan Lebire and Chato René Rivas Melara are trying to improve the lives of unhoused people in Milton Parc. Some leave the street and manage to rebuild their lives, but this street corner, unremarkable to some, remains the heart of their community.
